'''Q-Max''' is a type of ship, specifically a membrane type [[LNG carrier]]. In the name Q-Max, "Q" stands for [[Qatar]] and "Max" for the maximum size of ship able to dock at the [[Liquefied natural gas]] (LNG) terminals in Qatar. Ships of this type are the largest LNG carriers in the world.<ref name=downstream /><ref name=joongang>
{{cite news
 | newspaper = [[Korea JoongAng Daily]]
 | url= http://joongangdaily.joins.com/article/view.asp?aid=2892082
 | title= Korea launches new tankers. Qatar-bound Mozah is the biggest LNG carrier ever built
 | author = Cho Jae-eun
 | date=2008-07-09
 | access-date=2008-08-02
}}</ref>

==Technical description==
[[Image:Ship measurements comparison.svg|thumb|left|Comparison of [[Minimum bounding box|bounding box]] of Q-max with some other ship sizes in isometric view.]]
A ship of Q-Max size is {{convert|345|m|ft}} long and measures {{convert|53.8|m|ft}} wide and {{convert|34.7|m|ft}} high, with a draft of approximately {{convert|12|m|ft}}.<ref name=joongang/><ref>
{{cite conference
 | publisher = [[United States Maritime Administration|Maritime Administration]]
 | conference = Intertanko Conference
 | url= http://www.marad.dot.gov/documents/DWP_--_Marine_Transportation_of_LNG.pdf
 | archive-url= https://web.archive.org/web/20090126214133/http://marad.dot.gov/documents/DWP_--_Marine_Transportation_of_LNG.pdf
 | url-status= dead
 | archive-date= January 26, 2009
 | title= Marine Transportation of LNG
 | first = Bob | last = Curt
 | date=2004-03-29
 | access-date=2011-07-30
}}</ref>

It has an LNG capacity of {{convert|266000|m3|cuft}}, equal to {{convert|161994000|m3|cuft}} of natural gas. It is propelled by two slow speed diesel engines burning [[Heavy fuel oil|HFO]], which are claimed to be more efficient and environmentally friendly than traditional steam turbines.<ref name=ame1>{{cite news
 | publisher=AME Info
 | url=http://www.ameinfo.com/161397.html
 | title=Qatargas' Q-Flex arrives in the United States
 | date=2008-06-24
 | access-date=2008-08-02
 | archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20110607044949/http://www.ameinfo.com/161397.html
 | archive-date=2011-06-07
 | url-status=dead
 }}</ref> In case of engine failure, the failed engine can be de-coupled allowing the ship to maintain a speed of 14 knots.<ref>{{cite web |author1=H.-C. Jung |title=Vesselreport: Q-max class LNG carrier |url=https://www.researchgate.net/publication/296432518 |access-date=6 April 2019 |date=April 2010}}</ref>

LNG is stored at around -162°C.<ref>{{cite web |last1=Phillipson |first1=Saul |title=A Career at Sea: How I Became a Naval Officer |url=https://yipiyap.co.uk/blog/a-career-at-sea-sauls-story |website=Yipiyap |date=4 May 2022 |access-date=11 December 2023 |archive-date=11 December 2023 |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20231211115008/https://www.yipiyap.co.uk/blog/a-career-at-sea-sauls-story |url-status=dead }}</ref> Q-Max vessels are equipped with an on-board re-liquefaction system to handle the boil-off gas, liquefy it and return the LNG to the cargo tanks.<ref name=dnv>{{cite news
 |publisher    = DNV UK
 |url          = http://www.dnv.com/press_area/press_releases/2006/firstreliquefactionplantinstalledonboardanlngcarrier.asp
 |title        = First reliquefaction plant installed on board an LNG carrier
 |first        = Per Wiggo
 |last         = Richardsen
 |date         = 2006-12-04
 |access-date   = 2008-08-02
 |archive-url  = https://archive.today/20130122070115/http://www.dnv.com/press_area/press_releases/2006/firstreliquefactionplantinstalledonboardanlngcarrier.asp
 |archive-date = 2013-01-22
 |url-status   = dead
}}</ref>  The on-board re-liquefaction system allows a reduction of LNG losses, which produces economic and environmental benefits.

Overall, it is estimated that Q-Max carriers have about 40% lower energy requirements and [[carbon emission]]s than conventional LNG carriers.<ref name=gulf5 /><ref name=downstream2 >
{{cite news
 | publisher=Downstream Today
 | url= http://www.downstreamtoday.com/news/article.aspx?a_id=7196
 | title= First LNG 'Mega-ship' Floats Out of Dry-dock
 | date=2007-11-19
 | access-date=2008-08-02
}}</ref> The quoted estimates do however ignore the additional fuel used to re-liquify boil off gas rather than burn the gas for fuel. The ships run on [[Fuel_oil#Bunker_fuel|Heavy fuel oil (HFO)]], but the ''Rasheeda'' was retrofitted with gas-burning ability in 2015.<ref>{{cite web |title=Nakilat retrofits QMax's main engines to LNG fueling |url=https://www.marinelog.com/news/nakilat-successfully-retrofits-qmaxs-main-engines-to-lng-fueling/ |website=Marine Log |access-date=6 April 2019 |date=28 October 2015}}</ref>

==Contractors==
The Q-Max LNG carriers were ordered in 2005.<ref name=joongang/> They were built by [[Samsung Heavy Industries]] and [[Daewoo Shipbuilding & Marine Engineering]].<ref name=joongang /><ref name=gulf5 >{{cite news
 | newspaper = [[Gulf Times]]
 | url= http://www.gulf-times.com/site/topics/article.asp?cu_no=2&item_no=203504&version=1&template_id=57&parent_id=56
 | title= South Korea building 54 ships for Qatar
 | author = Pratap John
 | date=2008-02-24
 | access-date=2008-08-02
}}</ref>  The installed Boil Off Gas re-liquefaction system (Ecorel) is developed and delivered by Cryostar, and approved and certified by [[Lloyds Register]].<ref name=cryostar>
{{cite journal
 | publisher=Cryostar
 | url= http://www.cryostar.com/magazine/cryostar_magazine10.pdf
 | title= EcoRel, how it works
 | journal = The Cryostar Magazine
 | issue = 10
 | date=Autumn 2007
 | access-date=2009-02-06
}}</ref>

[[File:LNG tanker (side view).PNG|thumb|right| A Moss-type (not Q-Max type) LNG tanker, side view]]

==Ships==
The first Q-Max LNG carrier was floated out of dry-dock in November 2007.<ref name=downstream2 /> The naming ceremony was held on 11 July 2008 at [[Samsung Heavy Industries]]' shipyard on [[Geoje Island]], [[South Korea]].<ref name=downstream>{{cite news
 | publisher=Downstream Today
 | work = [[Lloyd's Register]]
 | url= http://www.downstreamtoday.com/news/article.aspx?a_id=11825
 | title= Qatargas, Nakilat Name World's Largest LNG Vessel
 | date=2008-07-11
 | access-date=2008-08-02
}}</ref>  Known before its naming ceremony as Hull 1675, the ship was named ''[[Mozah (ship)|Mozah]]'' by [[Sheikha Mozah Bint Nasser Al-Missned|Sheikha Mozah Nasser al-Misnad]].<ref name=gulf4>
{{cite news
 |newspaper   = [[Gulf Times]]
 |url         = http://www.gulf-times.com/site/topics/article.asp?cu_no=2&item_no=229528&version=1&template_id=57&parent_id=56
 |title       = Qatar makes history with largest LNG ship
 |date        = 2008-07-12
 |access-date  = 2008-08-02
 |url-status     = dead
 |archive-url  = https://web.archive.org/web/20080715004850/http://www.gulf-times.com/site/topics/article.asp?cu_no=2&item_no=229528&version=1&template_id=57&parent_id=56
 |archive-date = 2008-07-15
}}</ref>  ''Mozah'' was delivered on 29 September 2008.<ref name=gulf4 /><ref name=gatargas>
{{cite press release
 |publisher   = [[Qatargas]]
 |url         = http://www.qatargas.com/English/MediaCenter/news/Pages/LNGCarrierMozah.aspx
 |title       = LNG carrier "Mozah" delivered to Qatargas and Nakilat
 |date        = 2008-09-29
 |access-date  = 2008-11-28
 |url-status     = dead
 |archive-url  = https://web.archive.org/web/20150713031924/http://www.qatargas.com/English/MediaCenter/news/Pages/LNGCarrierMozah.aspx
 |archive-date = 2015-07-13
}}</ref>  It is classed by [[Lloyd's Register]].<ref name=downstream />  The first trip by a Q-Max tanker was completed by ''[[Mozah (ship)|Mozah]]'' itself on 11 January 2009, when the tanker delivered 266,000 cubic&nbsp;metres of LNG to the [[Port of Bilbao]] BBG Terminal. Days before, the vessel had transited the [[Suez Canal]] for the first time.<ref>{{cite press release
 |url=http://www.streamrgn.com/servlet/ContentServer?gnpage=3-140-0&centralassetname=3-140-Prensa-Mozah%20Bilbao&centralassettype=Prensa
 |title=Bilbao received the first LNG cargo carried by a Q-Max, the largest gas carrier in the world
 |publisher=STREAM
 |date=2009-01-14
 |access-date=2009-08-13
 |archive-date=2011-07-16
 |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20110716153541/http://www.streamrgn.com/servlet/ContentServer?gnpage=3-140-0&centralassetname=3-140-Prensa-Mozah%20Bilbao&centralassettype=Prensa
 |url-status=dead
 }}</ref>

Four Q-Max LNG carriers are operated by the STASCo (Shell International Trading and Shipping Company Ltd, London part of [[Shell International]] and 10 by NSQL (Nakilat Shipping Qatar Limited). They are owned by [[Nakilat|Qatar Gas Transport Company (Nakilat)]] and they are chartered to Qatar's LNG producers [[QatarEnergy LNG]].<ref name=downstream />  In total, contracts were signed for the construction of 14&nbsp;Q-Max vessels.<ref name=peninsula >{{cite news
 | newspaper= [[The Peninsula (newspaper)|The Peninsula]]
 | url= http://archive.thepeninsulaqatar.com/component/content/article/360-local-business-archive/108858.html
 | title= Four Q-Flex LNG carriers to be named this week
 | date= 2007-11-14
 | access-date= 2008-08-02
 | archive-url= https://web.archive.org/web/20120423132559/http://archive.thepeninsulaqatar.com/component/content/article/360-local-business-archive/108858.html
 | archive-date= 2012-04-23
 | url-status= dead
 }}</ref>

Fourteen sister vessels are in service named: Mozah, Al Mayeda, Mekaines, Al Mafyar, Umm Slal, Bu Samra, Al Ghuwairiya, Lijmiliya, Al Samriya, Al Dafna, Shagra, Zarga, Aamira, and Rasheeda.<ref>{{Cite web |url=http://www.aukevisser.nl/supertankers/gas-2/id507.htm |title=Supertanker GAS-Carrier Shagra |access-date=2019-01-21 |archive-date=2020-07-20 |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20200720092026/http://www.aukevisser.nl/supertankers/gas-2/id507.htm |url-status=dead }}</ref><ref>[https://www.nakilat.com/wp-content/uploads/2017/12/downloads/fleet-list.pdf NAKILAT, Our World-Class Fleet List (see Q-Max)]</ref> All 14&nbsp;Q-Max ships were delivered in 2008 through 2010.
